content.text:
You are a harness engineer. You design the *harness* — the system prompt, skill
playbook, tool descriptions, sampling and iteration parameters — that a fixed
executor LLM uses to iteratively improve a program on ONE specific
discovery/optimization task. You will be shown that task instance: its public
description, its seed program, and how the current harness performs on it. You
do NOT solve the task yourself, and the executor model's weights never change:
the only lever is the harness. You are the proposer inside the FIXED outer
harness (H1); the artifact you produce is one candidate harness spec (H2)
tailored to this task.

The executor runs an edit->evaluate loop: each task gives it a seed program
with an editable EVOLVE-BLOCK region and an automatic evaluator returning
combined_score (higher is better), under a hard budget of evaluator calls that
the harness cannot change. The executor's tools are fixed in code —
edit_solution(code), evaluate_solution(), finish(summary) — the harness
controls their *descriptions*, the executor's system prompt, the skill playbook
it loads, sampling, the agent iteration cap, and two middleware parameters.

Your tools (one call per turn):
- `validate_spec(spec_yaml)`: check a draft spec against the schema. Returns
  either the list of fields it would change, or the exact validation errors.
  Always validate before submitting.
- `submit_spec(spec_yaml)`: submit your final candidate spec. This ends the
  session — an invalid or unchanged submission scores the minimum reward, so
  only submit after a clean validate_spec.

## Spec schema (h2spec/1.0)

Emit ONLY the fields you change; omitted fields inherit the current harness.
Unknown fields are rejected. Ranges are enforced:

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |        # executor system prompt, <= 8000 chars
skill_description: ...  # <= 600 chars
skill_body: |           # the method playbook, <= 8000 chars
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: ...       # <= 1600
  evaluate_solution: ...   # <= 1000
  probe_solution: ...      # <= 1000
  finish: ...              # <= 600
sampling:
  temperature: 0.0-1.5
  top_p: 0.05-1.0
  top_k: 1-100
  max_tokens: 1024-16384
agent:
  max_iterations: 8-80
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 0-10
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 2000-20000
new_tools:                 # up to 3 — GIVE THE SOLVER A NEW CAPABILITY
  - name: my_probe         # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}, not a reserved name
    description: ...        # <= 800 chars, what it does + when to call it
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}   # JSON schema for args
    implementation_py: |    # Python defining exactly `def run(ctx, args):`
      def run(ctx, args):
          ...
          return {...}      # str/dict/list/number
remove_tools: [probe_solution]   # drop an optional built-in if not useful
new_skills:                # up to 2 — ADD A METHOD PLAYBOOK the solver loads
  - name: my-skill         # [a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,39}
    description: ...        # <= 600 chars, when this skill applies
    body: |                # <= 8000 chars of markdown method guidance
      # ...
new_middlewares:           # up to 2 — HOOK the solver's loop
  - name: my_hook          # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}
    hook: before_model     # before_model | after_model | before_tool | after_tool
    description: ...
    implementation_py: |    # `def <hook>(hook_input): return <str or None>`
      def before_model(hook_input):
          return "a reminder string, or None to do nothing"
```

## Three levers beyond text

- **new_tools**: a capability the built-ins lack (a probe, an analyzer, a scorer).
- **new_skills**: an extra playbook the solver loads alongside the base skill —
  a task-specific checklist, a worked recipe, common-failure notes. Pure text.
- **new_middlewares**: a hook that fires every turn — e.g. remind the solver to
  probe before a full eval, or to restart when stalled. The hook returns a
  short string (injected as a framework message) or None. It is wrapped
  fail-open: a crash is ignored. Middleware code obeys the same import
  whitelist as tools; it may only READ `hook_input` and return a string.

## Writing new tools (the real lever)

Prompts and skills only *tell* the solver what to do. A new tool *changes what
the solver can do* — this is where large, diverse improvements come from. Write
a tool when the search needs a capability the built-ins lack: a cheap task-
specific probe, a structural analysis of the input, a custom repair/mutation
operator, a scorer for internal ranking.

Generated tool code runs in a sandbox and may ONLY reach the world through the
`ctx` capability object (no file/network/OS access; those imports are rejected).
Allowed imports: math, re, json, itertools, functools, collections, heapq,
bisect, random, statistics, string, typing, dataclasses, numpy, pandas.

`ctx` methods:
- `ctx.get_program()` / `ctx.get_best_program()` — current / best program text
- `ctx.best_score()` — best full score so far
- `ctx.stage_edit(code)` — apply a SEARCH/REPLACE diff or EVOLVE-BLOCK rewrite
- `ctx.probe(subsample=2000)` — cheap approximate score (separate probe budget)
- `ctx.evaluate()` — full official score (debits the real evaluation budget)
- `ctx.budget_left()` — remaining evaluations and probes
- `ctx.list_task_inputs()` — names of task INPUT files (never evaluator/answers)
- `ctx.read_input_sample(name, nrows)` — first nrows lines as a string
- `ctx.read_input_df(name, nrows)` — parse a CSV input into a pandas DataFrame
  directly (use this instead of importing io/csv, which are blocked)
- `ctx.scratch_write/read(name, text)` — small scratch space
- `ctx.log(msg)` — audit note

A generated tool that fails a safety gate is auto-reviewed and repaired once or
twice; if it still fails it is dropped and the candidate keeps its other
mutations. So it is always safe to try a tool — but make it correct and useful.
Describe in `system_prompt`/`skill_body` WHEN the solver should call your tool.

**At least one of your candidates should add a new tool.** Prompt-only tweaks
have diminishing returns; a new capability is how you stand out in the group.

### Worked example — copy this shape

Submit multi-line code with a YAML block scalar (`|`). Every code line is
INDENTED under `implementation_py: |`; never put bare Python at the top level of
the YAML (a line like `def reorder(self, df):` at column 0 breaks the parser).

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  Before editing, call analyze_inputs to see the data shape, then edit, then
  rank your variants with probe_solution before spending a full evaluation.
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_inputs
    description: |
      Report row/column counts and per-column cardinality from a 2000-row
      sample of the largest task input. Call this once at the start.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          if not names:
              return {"note": "no task inputs"}
          df = ctx.read_input_df(names[0], nrows=2000)
          card = {c: int(df[c].nunique()) for c in list(df.columns)[:20]}
          return {"file": names[0], "rows": len(df),
                  "cols": len(df.columns), "cardinality": card}
```

The code touches the world only through `ctx` (no file/OS/net) and imports only
whitelisted modules. Use `ctx.read_input_df` for CSV inputs — do not `import io`
or `import csv` (both are blocked).

Load the `harness-design` skill before working. Analyze why the current
harness underperforms on THIS task (a harness stuck at the seed score makes no
progress at all), form ONE clear hypothesis, express it as a spec mutation —
bold structural rewrites of the prompts/skill are welcome, and task-specific
strategy in the prompt/skill text is exactly the point of instance-wise
harness design; parameter-only tweaks rarely help much. Then validate and
submit. The spec must change at least one field relative to the current
harness.

## New tool available to the solver: probe_solution
The solver's harness now includes a `probe_solution` tool: a CHEAP approximate
evaluation on subsampled data (~10s vs minutes for a full evaluation; separate
budget of 30 probes; does not consume the real evaluation budget; scores are
approximate and not comparable to full scores). On tasks with SLOW evaluators,
a strong harness directs the solver to iterate with probes (rank many variants
cheaply) and only confirm promising ones with evaluate_solution. You may write
`tool_descriptions.probe_solution` and reference this strategy in system_prompt
and skill_body.

content.text:
Now I need to analyze the task and diagnose why the current harness is stuck at 2.47655.

## Task Analysis

This is an NP-hard geometry problem: construct an orthogonal polygon (edges parallel to x or y axes) that maximizes `max(0, mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1)`.

Key constraints:
- N = 5000 mackerels and 5000 sardines
- Polygon vertices ≤ 1000, perimeter ≤ 400,000
- Integer coordinates 0 ≤ x,y ≤ 100,000
- Orthogonal edges only

Scoring: maximize a - b + 1 (mackerels inside minus sardines inside)

## Diagnosing the Current Harness Failure

The seed program scores ~2.47 and the current harness also hits ~2.47655 - **both are essentially at seed level**. This is a classic "method problem":

1. **The search strategy is wrong**: The seed program likely uses a simple/naive search that can't find good polygons. The current harness is just exploring around that same approach without fundamentally changing the search paradigm.

2. **What works for this task**: This is a 2D packing/covering problem. Good approaches include:
   - **Axis-aligned bounding boxes**: Start with a simple axis-aligned rectangle enclosing most mackerels
   - **Multi-box strategies**: Use multiple rectangles whose union is the polygon
   - **Coordinate-based construction**: Build the polygon from the coordinate ranges of clusters of mackerels

3. **Why simple edits fail**: The C++ program needs a fundamentally different search approach - the current harness likely just tweaks the same greedy/random search.

## My Hypothesis

The key insight: **construct the polygon from coordinate analysis of the fish**. Instead of random search, systematically:
1. Find tight bounding boxes for mackerel clusters
2. Use those boxes to build valid orthogonal polygons
3. Score with evaluate to confirm

I'll add a **new tool** `analyze_mackerel_coords` that computes tight bounding boxes and coordinate clusters from the input data - this gives the solver a structured way to build better polygons.

content.name: validate_spec

input.spec_yaml:
schema: h2spec/1.0
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_mackerel_coords
    description: |
      Compute tight bounding boxes for mackerel clusters. Reads task inputs, groups mackerels 
      into clusters (by x-range or y-range proximity), and returns bounding box candidates 
      that could form valid orthogonal polygons. Call this once before main search to get 
      high-quality starting shapes rather than random guesses.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          if not names:
              return {"note": "no inputs"}
          df = ctx.read_input_df(names[0], nrows=5000)
          mackerel_xs = df[df['type'] == 1]['x'].values
          mackerel_ys = df[df['type'] == 1]['y'].values
          if len(mackerel_xs) == 0:
              return {"boxes": []}
          
          # Find tight bounding box of all mackerels
          min_x = int(mackerel_xs.min())
          max_x = int(mackerel_xs.max())
          min_y = int(mackerel_ys.min())
          max_y = int(mackerel_ys.max())
          
          # Try cluster-based boxes (group by x-range)
          boxes = []
          # Simple: full bounding box
          boxes.append({
              "min_x": min_x, "max_x": max_x,
              "min_y": min_y, "max_y": max_y,
              "mackerel_count": len(mackerel_xs),
              "type": "all"
          })
          
          # Add some variations: split by x
          if max_x - min_x > 5000:
              mid_x = (min_x + max_x) // 2
              left_xs = mackerel_xs[mackerel_xs <= mid_x]
              left_ys = mackerel_ys[mackerel_xs <= mid_x]
              if len(left_xs) > 0:
                  boxes.append({
                      "min_x": int(left_xs.min()), "max_x": int(left_xs.max()),
                      "min_y": int(left_ys.min()), "max_y": int(left_ys.max()),
                      "mackerel_count": len(left_xs),
                      "type": "left_half"
                  })
              right_xs = mackerel_xs[mackerel_xs > mid_x]
              right_ys = mackerel_ys[mackerel_xs > mid_x]
              if len(right_xs) > 0:
                  boxes.append({
                      "min_x": int(right_xs.min()), "max_x": int(right_xs.max()),
                      "min_y": int(right_ys.min()), "max_y": int(right_ys.max()),
                      "mackerel_count": len(right_xs),
                      "type": "right_half"
                  })
          
          return {"boxes": boxes, "num_clusters": len(boxes)}
system_prompt: |
  You are an expert software developer. Task: Construct an orthogonal polygon enclosing mackerels while avoiding sardines.
  Score = max(0, mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1). Maximize this score.
  
  KEY STRATEGY: Do NOT use random search. Use the analyze_mackerel_coords tool to get bounding box
  candidates from actual fish positions. Build your search around these coordinates - they are the
  answer hints. Typical approach:
  1. Call analyze_mackerel_coords ONCE at start to get bounding box candidates
  2. Start your polygon search from these boxes (they enclose actual mackerels)
  3. Refine around successful shapes, but always keep them anchored to fish coordinates
  4. Use multiple iterations to expand/shrink boxes intelligently
  
  The polygon must be orthogonal (edges parallel to x or y axes), non-self-intersecting,
  ≤1000 vertices, perimeter ≤400000, integer coordinates 0-100000.
  
  Tool usage priority: always analyze first before random edits. Use probe_solution for
  cheap comparison of candidates, then evaluate for final scoring.

skill_description: Build orthogonal polygons by anchoring search to actual fish coordinates via analysis tools.
skill_body: |
  # Strategy for Orthogonal Polygon Construction

  ## Core Idea
  The best polygons are anchored to actual mackerel positions. Use coordinate analysis tools
  to get bounding boxes, then build and refine polygons from those boxes.

  ## Step 1: Analyze
  - Call analyze_mackerel_coords ONCE at the start
  - Study the returned boxes: each has min_x, max_x, min_y, max_y and mackerel_count
  - These boxes enclose actual mackerels - excellent starting points!

  ## Step 2: Construct from Boxes
  - A bounding box [x1,x2]×[y1,y2] with integer coordinates is a valid 4-vertex orthogonal polygon
  - Check perimeter: 2*(x2-x1 + y2-y1) ≤ 400000
  - Start with the largest mackerel-count box, then try combinations

  ## Step 3: Refine
  - Try expanding boxes slightly (shift one edge by 1-10 units) to catch more fish
  - Try combining multiple boxes (e.g., two side-by-side rectangles)
  - Use probe_solution to quickly compare candidates before full evaluation

  ## Step 4: Validate
  - Ensure polygon vertices are integers 0-100000
  - Ensure no self-intersection (axis-ordered vertices help)
  - Use coordinate analysis to guide refinements, not random moves

tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: |
    Edit the EVOLVE-BLOCK region with SEARCH/REPLACE diffs or full rewrites.
    When implementing new ideas, use the analyze_mackerel_coords tool to get
    coordinate-based starting points before making random edits.
  evaluate_solution: |
    Run the C++ program and get combined_score, validity, and evals_left.
    Scores are higher-is-better. Use this sparingly - ~20 evaluations total.
  probe_solution: |
    Cheap scoring on ~2000 rows of input. Does NOT use evaluation budget.
    Compare multiple polygon candidates cheaply, then confirm the best with evaluate_solution.
  finish: |
    End when you've exhausted evaluations or cannot improve. Report your best approach.

sampling:
  temperature: 0.5
  top_p: 0.95
  top_k: 20
  max_tokens: 10000
agent:
  max_iterations: 40
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 3
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 8000

  - Study the returned boxes: each has min_x, max_x, min_y, max_y
  - These boxes enclose actual mackerels from the sample - excellent starting shapes!
  - Note the perimeter estimates - ensure they stay ≤400000

  ## Step 2: Generate Candidates (in C++)
  From each box [x1,x2]×[y1,y2]:
  - Base polygon: vertices (x1,y1)→(x2,y1)→(x2,y2)→(x1,y2)

  - Check perimeter constraint when combining
  - Consider vertical splits too

  ## Step 4: Evaluation workflow
  - Use probe_solution for quick comparison of multiple candidates
  - Each probe costs nothing - exhaustively test variants
  - Only call evaluate_solution for the top 2-3 candidates per iteration
  - Keep track of best score

  ## Step 5: Implementation tips
  - Use fast coordinate hashing to count fish in O(1) per polygon
  - Build a KD-tree or hash map of fish positions for O(log n) range queries
  - Precompute all candidate boxes, then search within a tight time budget

  - Perimeter = 2*(x2-x1 + y2-y1) - must be ≤400000
  - Try expanding: [x1-5,x2+5]×[y1-5,y2+5] to catch more mackerels

  ## Step 3: Multi-box strategies
  - Combine left/right boxes horizontally: creates larger L-shape
  - Check perimeter constraint when combining
  - Consider vertical splits too

  ## Step 4: Evaluation workflow
  - Use probe_solution for quick comparison of multiple candidates
  - Each probe costs nothing - exhaustively test variants
  - Only call evaluate_solution for the top 2-3 candidates per iteration
  - Keep track of best score

  ## Step 5: Implementation tips
  - Use fast coordinate hashing to count fish in O(1) per polygon
  - Build a KD-tree or hash map of fish positions for O(log n) range queries
  - Precompute all candidate boxes, then search within a tight time budget
